column1: What is the foundational invariant of sed's execution model regarding how much of the input it sees at once?
column2: Sed never sees the whole file at once; it operates one record (line) at a time, enabling constant memory usage regardless of file size.

column1: What are the two string buffers sed maintains across its lifetime, and how do their persistence semantics differ?
column2: The pattern space (working register, loaded each cycle and cleared after printing) and the hold space (persistent accumulator, unchanged across cycles unless explicitly written to).

column1: What is the 'implicit print' in sed, and what disables it?
column2: The automatic printing of the pattern space's contents at the end of each cycle before it is cleared; it is suppressed by the -n flag.

column1: Describe the full sed execution cycle for one line of input.
column2: Read one line into the pattern space → execute all script commands against it → (unless -n) print the pattern space → clear the pattern space → advance to the next line and repeat.

column1: Why is sed's memory consumption bounded by line size rather than file size?
column2: Because sed's single-pass architecture never materializes the whole file in memory; it only holds the current pattern space (and hold space) buffers, whose size is bounded by the largest line processed.

column1: What key architectural limitation results from sed's single-pass, line-oriented model?
column2: Sed is architecturally incapable of random access — it cannot jump to an arbitrary line and back, nor hold an arbitrary number of lines in memory simultaneously.

column1: What common misconception do engineers have about what sed fundamentally is?
column2: They treat sed as merely a find-and-replace tool, when it is actually a Turing-complete-within-limits scripting language with an address-based conditional dispatch mechanism, two registers, and branch/label facilities.

column1: In sed, what condition must be true for the `t` command to branch to its label?
column2: The `t` command branches only if a successful substitution has occurred since the last line was read or since the last `t` test was evaluated.

column1: How does sed implement iteration/looping, given it has no native loop construct?
column2: Through the combination of a substitution command, the conditional branch `t`, and a `:label` jump target, which together implement bounded repetition.

column1: What is the difference between sed's `b` and `t` commands?
column2: `b` is an unconditional branch to a label; `t` is a conditional branch that only triggers if a substitution succeeded since the last line read or last `t` test.

column1: Why must the hold space be understood as central to multi-line processing in sed?
column2: Because unlike the pattern space (wiped each cycle), the hold space persists across cycles, allowing content from prior lines to be carried forward for reversal, accumulation, or deferred output.

column1: When compiling GNU sed from source for debugging/profiling labs, why use `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` alongside `-O1`?
column2: `-O1` preserves realistic optimization without collapsing the call graph via excessive inlining, while `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` keeps `rbp` as a true frame pointer so `perf record` can walk the stack without costly, distorting DWARF unwinding.
